title: Measuring Agents in Production
one_liner: Study how deployed language-model agents are really built, checked, and kept under control once they are running in real organizations.
lead: This paper is not a new agent training method. It is a measurement study of systems that are already in use. The authors interview builders and survey practitioners to find out what kinds of agent designs survive contact with real work, what teams care about when they judge success, and what keeps failing after deployment. The main message is that production agents are usually short-horizon systems with strong human oversight because teams trade freedom for control.

problem.h2: Why production agent practice is hard to see from papers alone
paras: A research paper can show a strong demo, yet that does not tell you what companies actually keep in production. Real deployments face approval rules, cost limits, handoff needs, and users who will stop trusting the system after a few bad outcomes.

Without direct evidence from deployed systems, researchers can aim at the wrong target. They may study long open-ended agents while most real teams use shorter flows with checkpoints because those flows are easier to check, pause, and repair.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Measure live deployment practice directly through interviews and surveys so that agent research can be compared against the constraints that real teams face.

panels.title: 1. Teams want automation
panels.viz_args: Organizations adopt agents to save staff time and cover repetitive work
panels.caption: The goal is useful work completion, not a lab score.

panels.title: 2. Real limits appear
panels.viz_args: Wrong actions, long runs, and weak checks create business risk
panels.caption: A system that looks capable in a demo may still be too risky to run freely.

panels.title: 3. Builders narrow the design
panels.caption: Teams keep the parts they can monitor closely because they need steady behavior over time.

panels.title: 4. Evaluation stays human-centered
panels.viz_args: Teams inspect outputs and failure cases by hand
panels.caption: Human review remains common because many failures depend on context that simple automatic scores miss.

panels.title: 5. The field gets a reality check
panels.caption: The study shows which agent choices are common in practice and which research gaps still matter.

steps.text: Interview 20 teams in depth so that the study captures how deployed agents are assembled and operated.
Ask 86 practitioners across many domains what they build, how they check it, and where it fails.
Measure step limits, prompting use, weight tuning use, and human review so that the study reflects common system patterns.
Track why organizations adopt agents and what blocks wider deployment because the mismatch reveals open engineering problems.
Turn those observations into a map of current production practice so that future agent work can target real constraints.

paras: The paper changes our picture of what an agent system usually looks like after deployment. Instead of assuming that high autonomy is the default target, it shows that many teams purposely constrain the agent because constraint makes behavior easier to predict and easier to review.
object.object: the field's estimate of the autonomy level that production teams actually use

hidden.name: how much uncertainty a team is willing to tolerate from an agent
paras: The central hidden quantity is the tolerance for uncertain behavior inside a real organization. A deployed agent is not judged only by whether it can finish a task once. It is judged by whether teams can trust it to behave acceptably over many runs.

This quantity does not appear as one number in a dashboard. You infer it from design choices such as step caps, required human approval, and reliance on prompt control because those choices reveal how much freedom the team is comfortable granting.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark choices that often reveal how tightly a team wants to control the agent.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is how much freedom a team believes it can safely give the agent.
The study recovers that hidden tolerance by observing the system limits and evaluation habits that deployed teams choose.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: deployment choices reveal the real target
paras: If you ask teams what they want, they may describe an ambitious long-term vision. If you inspect the system they actually run, you see the design compromises they accepted because those compromises are what passed operational review.

That is why direct field measurement matters here. Interviews and surveys expose which choices repeat across domains. When many teams independently limit step count, favor prompt control, and keep human review, the pattern suggests that these choices solve a shared problem: they reduce unpredictable behavior by keeping the system easier to inspect and interrupt.

stages.s: Deployed agent teams with real operating constraints
Observe how they build and review the system
Find recurring choices such as step caps and human checks
Interpret those choices as control strategies because they manage deployment risk
A grounded view of what production agent practice currently values

math.h2: Summarize production practice as weighted evidence from teams
math.words: A simple summary is to treat each survey or interview response as evidence about one deployment choice, then average those choices across teams. The larger the average for a choice, the more common that choice is in production practice.
symbols: average prevalence of one deployment choice across teams
number of teams or respondents included in the measurement
1 when team i uses that choice and 0 otherwise

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: If 60 of them require human review for their main agent flow, the score for human review is 60 divided by 86.
The high score matters because it shows the choice is common across deployed systems.

math.note: The paper reports several percentages directly, and this average captures the basic measurement idea behind those summaries.

charts.title: Common production choices
charts.note: These counts matter because they show which choices are common when teams care about control and day-to-day operation.

charts.title: Main deployment pressure
charts.note: Reliability stays dominant because teams need consistent acceptable behavior over time, not only isolated wins.

items.html: A team may underreport problems or may not notice certain user harms, so the study can inherit blind spots from the practitioners it surveys.

items.b: Current practice is not the final destination.
items.html: A common design choice today may reflect present tool limits rather than an ideal long-term design, so the study should guide research without freezing it.

items.b: Domain mix can skew the picture.
items.html: If some industries are overrepresented, the aggregate view can lean toward their needs because those teams contribute more evidence to the summary.
The study is useful because it tells the field what builders are actually optimizing for once the agent has to survive routine use.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small dashboard that compares two kinds of agent deployments: a short tightly controlled flow and a longer more autonomous flow. For each one, log step count, required human approvals, output error rate, and how often operators intervene.

The demo should make the tradeoff visible by showing that tighter control often reduces operational surprises because the system has more checkpoints where a person can stop or redirect it. Pair the dashboard with a short practitioner survey so that technical measurements and operator judgment can be viewed together.
demo.metric_eq: control_gap = intervention_rate_long_flow - intervention_rate_short_flow ; review_share = reviewed_runs / total_runs
demo.closing: The point is to show how deployment teams choose designs that stay manageable under daily use.
